# AF 第九章 原文（重制基线）

## Chapter 9

[P01] Boxer's split（分裂） hoof took a long time to get better. They began to build the windmill（风车） again the day after the victory celebrations（庆祝）. Boxer would not take even one day off. He felt it was a matter of honour to hide his pain. In the evenings he told Clover that the hoof troubled him a lot. Clover treated it with poultices（药膏） of herbs（草药）. She and Benjamin both asked Boxer to work less hard. "A horse's lungs（肺） do not last for ever," she said. But Boxer would not listen.

[P02] He said he had only one real wish left—to see the windmill well under way before he was too old to work. At the start, the retiring（退休） age was twelve for horses and pigs, fourteen for cows, nine for dogs, seven for sheep, and five for hens and geese. Pensions（养老金） were promised. No animal had yet retired（退休的）, but lately the subject came up more and more. Now the small field beyond the orchard（果园） was kept for barley（大麦）, so people said a corner of the big pasture（牧场） would be fenced off for old animals.

[P03] For a horse, the pension（养老金） would be five pounds of corn a day, and in winter fifteen pounds of hay（干草）, with a carrot or an apple on holidays. Boxer would turn twelve next year. Life was hard. The winter was as cold as before, and food was even less. Rations（配给） were cut again for all, except the pigs and the dogs. Squealer said equal rations would go against Animalism（动物主义）. Anyway, he easily proved to the other animals that in fact they were NOT short of food, no matter how things looked.

[P04] For now, they had to change the rations a bit (Squealer always called it a "readjustment（调整）," never a "reduction（减少）"), but compared with the days of Jones, life was much better. In a high, quick voice, he read out the numbers. He showed them that they had more oats（燕麦）, more hay, more turnips（萝卜） than in Jones's day. They worked shorter hours. Their water was better. They lived longer. More of their young ones lived past infancy（婴儿期）. They had more straw（稻草） in their stalls（畜栏） and fewer fleas（跳蚤）.

[P05] The animals believed every word of it. To tell the truth, Jones and all he stood for had almost faded from their memories. They knew that life these days was hard and plain, that they were often hungry and often cold, and that they were usually working when they were not asleep. But it had surely been worse in the old days. They were happy to believe so. Besides, in those days they had been slaves, and now they were free, and that made all the difference, as Squealer never failed to point out.

[P06] In the autumn the four sows（母猪） all gave birth at about the same time. Together they had thirty-one young pigs. The young pigs were piebald（花斑）, and Napoleon was the only boar（公猪）, so it was easy to guess their father. Later, after bricks（砖块） and wood were bought, a schoolroom（教室） would be built in the garden. For now, Napoleon taught the young pigs in the kitchen. They took exercise in the garden and were told not to play with other young animals. A rule was also made: when a pig met any other animal on the path（小路）, the other animal must stand aside（旁边）. Also, all pigs could wear green ribbons（丝带） on their tails on Sundays. The farm had a fairly good year, but was still short of money.

[P07] They had to buy bricks, sand, and lime（石灰） for the schoolroom, and start saving for the windmill machinery（机器）. There was also lamp oil, candles, sugar for Napoleon's own table (the other pigs were not allowed it, because it made them fat), and the usual things like tools, nails（钉子）, string, coal, wire（电线）, scrap（废料）-iron, and dog biscuits. They sold a stump（树桩） of hay and part of the potato crop, and the egg contract went up to six hundred a week, so the hens barely（几乎不） hatched（孵化） enough chicks to keep their numbers the same.

[P08] Rations were cut in December, then again in February, and lanterns in the stalls were banned（禁止） to save oil. But the pigs looked fine, and even fatter. One late February afternoon, a warm, rich, tasty（美味） smell, better than anything the animals knew, came across the yard from the small brew（酿造）-house beyond the kitchen. It had not been used in Jones's time. Someone said it was cooking barley. The animals sniffed（嗅） hungrily（饥饿地）, wondering if a warm mash（糊状饲料） was for their supper. But no warm mash came, and the next Sunday it was announced that all barley would now be kept for the pigs.

[P09] The field past the orchard was already planted with barley. Soon everyone knew that each pig now got a pint（品脱） of beer every day, and Napoleon himself got half a gallon（加仑）, always served to him in the Crown（王冠） Derby（德比） soup tureen（大碗）. But if there were hard things to bear, life now had more dignity（尊严） than before. There were more songs, more speeches, more marches. Napoleon ordered that once a week there should be a Spontaneous（自发的） Demonstration（示范）, to celebrate the struggles（斗争） and triumphs（胜利） of Animal Farm.

[P10] At the set time the animals stopped work and marched round the farm in military（军事） order. The pigs led, then the horses, the cows, the sheep, and the birds. The dogs flanked（侧翼） the line, and Napoleon's black cockerel（小公鸡） marched in front. Boxer and Clover always carried a green banner（横幅） between them marked with the hoof and the horn, and the words, "Long live Comrade（同志） Napoleon!" After that came poems in Napoleon's honour, a speech by Squealer about the latest rises in food production, and sometimes a shot from the gun.

[P11] The sheep were the biggest fans of the Spontaneous（自发的） Demonstration（示范）. If anyone complained that the Spontaneous Demonstration wasted time and meant a lot of standing around in the cold (as a few animals sometimes did, when no pigs or dogs were near), the sheep were sure to quiet him with a loud bleating of "Four legs good, two legs bad!"But mostly the animals enjoyed these celebrations. It made them feel good to be reminded that, after all, they were really their own masters, and that the work they did was for their own good. So with the songs, the marches, Squealer's lists of numbers, the thunder of the gun, the crowing（啼叫） of the cockerel, and the waving of the flag, they were able to forget that their bellies（腹部） were empty（空的）, at least part of the time.

[P12] Only one candidate（候选人）, Napoleon, and everyone voted for him. That same day, people said new papers had been found. These papers showed more about how Snowball had helped Jones. It now seemed Snowball had not just tried to lose the Battle of the Cowshed（牛棚） by a trick, as the animals had thought before. He had been fighting openly on Jones's side. In fact, he had been the leader of the human forces, and had run into battle crying "Long live Humanity（人类）!" The wounds on Snowball's back, which a few animals still remembered seeing, had been made by Napoleon's teeth. In the middle of the summer Moses the raven（乌鸦） suddenly came back to the farm, after being away for several years.

[P13] He looked the same, still did no work, and talked as before about Sugarcandy（糖块） Mountain. He would sit on a stump, move his black wings, and talk for hours to anyone who listened. "Up there, comrades（同志们）," he would say, pointing to the sky with his big beak（鸟嘴）—"just past that dark cloud—there it is, Sugarcandy（糖块） Mountain, that happy land where we poor animals will rest forever from our work!" He even said he had been there on a high flight, and had seen endless fields of clover, and linseed（亚麻籽） cake and lump（块） sugar growing on the hedges（树篱）.

[P14] Many animals believed him. Their lives now, they thought, were hungry and full of hard work. Was it not fair that a better world should be somewhere else? One thing was hard to know: what did the pigs think of Moses? They all said his stories about Sugarcandy Mountain were lies. Yet they let him stay on the farm, doing no work, with a gill（鳃） of beer every day. After his hoof（蹄） healed（治愈）, Boxer worked harder than ever. Indeed, all the animals worked like slaves that year. Apart from the usual farm work and the rebuilding of the windmill, there was the schoolhouse for the young pigs, which opened in March.

[P15] Sometimes the long hours and little food were hard to bear, but Boxer never gave up. In nothing he said or did was there any sign that his strength was less than before. Only his looks had changed a little; his hide was less shiny（闪亮） than it used to be, and his great haunches（臀部） seemed to have shrunken（萎缩）. The others said, "Boxer will get better when the spring grass comes on"; but the spring came and Boxer grew no fatter. Sometimes on the slope（斜坡） to the quarry（采石场） top, when he braced（撑住） his muscles（肌肉） against a huge boulder（巨石）, it seemed that only the will to go on kept him standing.

[P16] At these times his lips（嘴唇） moved to say, "I will work harder"; he had no voice left. Again Clover and Benjamin told him to rest, but Boxer did not listen. His twelfth birthday was near. He did not mind what happened if he stored enough stone before going on pension. Late one summer evening, a rumour（谣言） ran round the farm that something had happened to Boxer. He had gone out alone to pull a load（负载） of stone to the windmill. And the rumour was true. A few minutes later two pigeons came racing in with the news: "Boxer has fallen!

[P17] He is lying（躺） on his side and cannot get up! About half the animals rushed to the knoll（小丘） where the windmill stood. Boxer lay between the shafts（车辕） of the cart, his neck stretched（伸展） out. He could not raise his head. His eyes were dull（沉闷）, his sides wet with sweat（汗水）. A thin stream of blood came from his mouth. Clover dropped to her knees beside him. "Boxer!" she cried. "How are you?" "It is my lung（肺）," said Boxer in a weak voice. "It does not matter. I think you can finish the windmill without me.

[P18] There is a good pile of stone saved up. I only had one more month to work. To tell the truth, I was looking forward to my rest. And maybe, since Benjamin is getting old too, they will let him stop working and keep me company." "We must get help at once," said Clover. "Run, somebody, and tell Squealer." All the other animals raced back to the farmhouse（农舍） to give Squealer the news. Only Clover stayed, and Benjamin lay down at Boxer's side, and, without speaking, kept the flies off him with his long tail.

[P19] After about fifteen minutes Squealer came, full of pity. He said Comrade Napoleon had heard with deep sadness of this bad luck to one of the most loyal（忠诚） workers, and was planning to send Boxer to the hospital at Willingdon. The animals felt worried. Except for Mollie and Snowball, no other animal had ever left the farm, and they did not like to think of their sick comrade（同志） with human beings. However, Squealer made them believe that the animal doctor in Willingdon could treat Boxer better than the farm could.

[P20] About half an hour later, Boxer felt a little better. He got up with difficulty and limped（跛行） back to his stall（畜栏）, where Clover and Benjamin had made a bed of straw for him. For two days Boxer stayed in his stall. The pigs sent a big bottle of pink medicine from the bathroom chest, and Clover gave it to Boxer twice a day. In the evenings she lay in his stall and talked, while Benjamin kept the flies off. Boxer said he was not sorry for what had happened.

[P21] If he got better, he might live another three years, and he looked forward to peaceful（平静） days in the corner of the big pasture. It would be the first time he had free time to study and improve his mind. He said he wanted to spend the rest of his life learning the other twenty-two letters of the alphabet（字母表）. However, Benjamin and Clover could only be with Boxer after work, and it was in the middle of the day when the van（货车） came to take him away. The animals were all weeding（除草） turnips under a pig's watch, when they were surprised to see Benjamin come galloping（飞奔） from the farm buildings, braying（驴叫） loudly.

[P22] It was the first time they had seen Benjamin excited—and the first time anyone had seen him gallop（疾驰）. "Quick, quick!" he shouted. "Come at once! They're（他们是） taking Boxer away!" The animals did not wait for orders. They stopped work and ran back to the buildings. Sure enough, in the yard stood a big closed van with two horses, letters on its side, and a sly man in a low hat on the driver's seat. Boxer's stall was empty. The animals crowded round the van. "Good-bye, Boxer!" they sang together, "good-bye!" "Fools! Fools!" shouted Benjamin, jumping round them and stamping the earth with his small hoofs（蹄）.

[P23] "Fools! Do you not see what is written on the side of that van?" That made the animals stop and all was quiet. Muriel began to spell the words. But Benjamin pushed her away and in the dead silence he read: "'Alfred Simmonds, Horse Slaughterer and Glue Boiler, Willingdon. Seller of Hides and Bone-Meal. Dog Food Supplied.' Do you not understand? They are taking Boxer to the knacker（屠夫）'s!" A cry of horror（恐怖） burst（爆发） from all the animals. Then the man on the box whipped his horses and the van moved out of the yard at a quick trot（疾走）.

[P24] All the animals followed, shouting loudly. Clover pushed to the front. The van went faster. Clover tried to gallop, and got to a canter（慢跑）. "Boxer!" she cried. "Boxer! Boxer! Boxer!" Just then, as if he heard the noise, Boxer's face, with the white stripe down his nose, showed at the small back window."Boxer!" cried Clover. "Boxer! Get out! Get out quickly! They're（他们是） taking you to your death!" All the animals cried, "Get out, Boxer, get out!" But the van was going faster and pulling away.

[P25] It was not clear if Boxer understood Clover's words. But a moment later his face went from the window, and there was a tremendous（极大的） drumming（击鼓） of hoofs inside the van. He was trying to kick his way out. Once, a few kicks from Boxer's hoofs would have smashed（粉碎） the van. But alas（唉）! his strength had left him; soon the drumming grew fainter（更微弱） and died away. In desperation（绝望） the animals begged（乞求） the two horses that pulled the van to stop. "Comrades, comrades!" they shouted. "Don't（不） take your own brother to his death!" But the stupid brutes（畜生）, too foolish to understand, only put back their ears and went faster.

[P26] Boxer's face did not come back at the window. It was too late when someone thought of running ahead and closing the gate. Soon the van was lost down the road. Boxer was never seen again.

Three days later, the animals were told that he had died in the hospital at Willingdon, even though he had received every care. Squealer came to tell the others. He said he had been there during Boxer's last hours. "It was the most moving sight I have ever seen!" said Squealer, wiping（擦拭） away a tear. "I was at his bedside（床边） at the very last.

[P27] In the end, he was too weak to speak much. He whispered（低语） that his only sadness was to die before the windmill was finished. 'Forward, comrades!' he whispered. 'Forward in the name of the uprising（起义）. Long live Animal Farm! Long live Comrade Napoleon! Napoleon is always right.' Those were his last words, comrades." Here Squealer's demeanour suddenly changed. Then Squealer changed. He was silent, and his little eyes looked from side to side with doubt before he went on. He said a foolish and bad rumour had been spread when Boxer was taken away.

[P28] Some animals saw that the van which took Boxer away had "Horse Slaughterer（屠夫）" on it. They thought Boxer was sent to the knacker's. Squealer said it was almost unbelievable（难以置信） that any animal could be so stupid. He cried angrily（愤怒地）, moving his tail and jumping from side to side. Surely they knew their beloved（心爱的） Leader, Comrade Napoleon, better than that? But the answer was very simple. The van had belonged to the knacker before. The veterinary（兽医的） surgeon（外科医生） bought it, and he had not yet painted out the old name. That was how the mistake happened. The animals felt very glad to hear this.

[P29] Squealer then told them more details of Boxer's death-bed, the good care he had received, and the costly medicines Napoleon had paid for. Their last doubts went away, and their sorrow（悲伤） was softened（柔和） by the thought that at least he had died happy. Napoleon came to the meeting next Sunday morning and gave a short speech in Boxer's honour. He said they could not bring back their friend's body for burial（埋葬） on the farm, but he had ordered a large wreath（花圈） made from the laurels（月桂） in the farmhouse garden and sent to Boxer's grave（坟墓）.

[P30] In a few days, the pigs planned to hold a memorial（纪念碑） banquet（宴会） for Boxer. Napoleon ended his speech by recalling Boxer's two favourite sayings（谚语）, "I will work harder" and "Comrade Napoleon is always right"—sayings, he said, that every animal should make his own. On the chosen day, a grocer（杂货商）'s van came from Willingdon and left a big wooden crate（板条箱） at the farmhouse. That night there was loud singing, then what seemed like a fierce quarrel（争吵）, and it ended around eleven o'clock with a huge crash（碰撞） of glass. No one moved in the farmhouse before noon the next day, and word spread that the pigs had got money from somewhere to buy themselves another case of whisky（威士忌）.
